```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

This vignette forecasts several series at once: the rows a forecast needs,
a model whose forecasts carry each series on from where its data end, a
covariate whose future is not known, fan charts, and totals across series and
over the horizon. Along the way, a check on the model's trend finds something
to change, and the change is made.

```{r setup}
library(limn)
```

## The data

Six regions report their weekly demand for two years. Demand rises with the
temperature, grows slowly over time, and each region has runs of high and low
weeks. The temperature follows the seasons, with runs of warm and cool weeks of
its own.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
n_regions <- 6; n_weeks <- 104
demand <- expand.grid(week = 1:n_weeks, region = factor(sprintf("R%d", 1:n_regions)))
runs <- function(phi, sd) unlist(lapply(1:n_regions, function(r)
  as.numeric(stats::arima.sim(list(ar = phi), n_weeks, sd = sd))))
demand$temp <- round(15 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * demand$week / 52) + runs(0.7, 1.5), 1)
region_effect <- rnorm(n_regions, 0, 10)
demand$demand <- round(100 + 0.15 * demand$week + 2 * (demand$temp - 15) +
                         region_effect[demand$region] + runs(0.8, 2) +
                         rnorm(nrow(demand), 0, 2), 1)
```

## The rows a forecast needs

`ilm_future()` builds the next weeks of every region. It copies what does not
change over time and leaves what does, the temperature, for you to fill in:

```{r future}
future <- ilm_future(demand, time = "week", group = "region", h = 8, response = "demand")
head(future, 3)
```

For a start, fill in a scenario: the temperature's seasonal average, with no
warm or cool runs.

```{r scenario}
scenario <- future
scenario$temp <- round(15 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * scenario$week / 52), 1)
```

## A first model, and the trend check

A first model has the temperature, a linear trend in time, a level for each
region, and a first-order autoregressive term, `ilm_ar1()`, for each region's
runs of weeks. Forecasting with it warns:

```{r trend-ar1}
fit_ar1 <- illume::ilm_model(demand ~ temp + week + (1 | region), data = demand,
                             family = "gaussian", ar = illume::ilm_ar1(~ week | region),
                             verbose = FALSE)
fc_ar1 <- ilm_forecast(fit_ar1, scenario, nsim = 500)
```

A trend in the fixed part assumes the growth goes on at the same rate, and,
in limn's own reasoning, its intervals then leave out any change in that rate.
The warning names the remedy, citing Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021, section
10.4) for a stochastic trend being safer at longer horizons: a random walk,
`ilm_rw1()`, which lets each region's level move. Refit with it in place of the
autoregressive term, and forecast again:

```{r trend-rw1}
fit <- illume::ilm_model(demand ~ temp + week + (1 | region), data = demand,
                         family = "gaussian", ar = illume::ilm_rw1(~ week | region),
                         verbose = FALSE)
fc_scenario <- ilm_forecast(fit, scenario, nsim = 500)
```

No warning now. The width of region R1's 90% interval at each horizon shows
the difference:

```{r widths}
width_r1 <- function(fc) {
  a <- as.data.frame(fc)
  a <- a[a$region == "R1", ]
  setNames(round(a$upper_0.9 - a$lower_0.9, 1), paste0("h", a$horizon))
}
rbind(ar1 = width_r1(fc_ar1), rw1 = width_r1(fc_scenario))
```

For region R1, under the autoregressive term the intervals stop widening after
a few weeks; under the random walk they go on widening with the horizon. The
rest of this vignette uses the random-walk model.

## A covariate whose future is not known

The scenario fixed next weeks' temperatures, so its intervals leave out the
uncertainty in them. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021, section 10.3) note that
prediction intervals made that way "do not take into account the uncertainty
in the forecasts of the predictors". `ilm_covariate_paths()` draws the
temperature's future from a model of the temperature, one path per draw, and
the forecast mixes over the paths:

```{r paths}
fit_temp <- illume::ilm_model(temp ~ illume::ilm_fourier(week, period = 52), data = demand,
                              family = "gaussian", ar = illume::ilm_ar1(~ week | region),
                              verbose = FALSE)
paths <- ilm_covariate_paths(fit_temp, future, nsim = 500)
fc <- ilm_forecast(fit, paths, nsim = 500)
rbind(scenario = width_r1(fc_scenario), paths = width_r1(fc))
```

The temperature model has the seasons, as a Fourier term, and each region's
runs of warm and cool weeks. With the temperature drawn, region R1's
intervals are wider at every horizon. In limn's own study of covariates given
as draws (`studies/findings/covariate_draws.md` in limn's GitHub repository,
<https://github.com/huttoncp/limn/blob/main/studies/findings/covariate_draws.md>),
90% intervals for a gaussian outcome made with the covariate's point forecast
covered only 0.75 to 0.83, against about 0.90 with the covariate given as
draws.

### Paths from another tool

Paths made elsewhere, such as a weather service's ensemble, come in through
`ilm_as_draws()`. Here a made-up ensemble of 20 paths stands in for one: a
data frame with a row per path, region and week.

```{r ensemble}
ensemble <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:20, function(k) {
  e <- future[c("region", "week")]
  e$temp <- round(15 + 8 * sin(2 * pi * e$week / 52) + rnorm(nrow(e), 0, 2), 1)
  e$.rep <- k
  e
}))
from_ensemble <- ilm_as_draws(ensemble, future, by = c("region", "week"))
head(as.data.frame(ilm_forecast(fit, from_ensemble, nsim = 500)), 3)
```

## The fan chart

```{r fan, fig.height = 6}
ilm_plot_fan(fc, time = "week", group = "region",
             history = demand[demand$week > 74, ], response = "demand")
```

Each panel is one region: its last 30 weeks of demand, then the forecast's
median as a line, with its central 50%, 80% and 95% intervals as bands. Each
region starts from its own last weeks, and the bands widen with the horizon.

## Totals

The total over regions is not the sum of the regions' intervals.
`ilm_aggregate()` adds the forecasts draw by draw, so what the regions share
within a draw, the parameters of the demand model and of the temperature
model, carries into the total. The total
demand each week:

```{r total-week}
as.data.frame(ilm_aggregate(fc, by = "week"))
```

And each region's total over the eight weeks, where a region's own path
carries into its total:

```{r total-region}
as.data.frame(ilm_aggregate(fc, by = "region"))
```

Both sets of totals come from the same draws, so the regions' expected totals
sum to exactly the same grand total as the weeks' do:

```{r coherent}
c(by_week = sum(as.data.frame(ilm_aggregate(fc, by = "week"))$mean),
  by_region = sum(as.data.frame(ilm_aggregate(fc, by = "region"))$mean))
```
